cards.front: What are the three French words for “my”, used before a masculine noun, a feminine noun and a plural noun?
cards.answer: mon (masculine) / ma (feminine) / mes (plural)

cards.front: What six positive personality adjectives does this lesson give for describing someone in French?
cards.answer: sympa / sympathique (nice) / gentil(le) (kind) / amusant(e) (funny) / intelligent(e) (clever) / sérieux/sérieuse (hardworking) / drôle (funny)

cards.front: Why is “sa sœur” used for both “his sister” and “her sister” in French?
cards.answer: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they describe, not the owner, so sa matches the feminine noun sœur either way.

cards.front: Why do you write “mon amie” rather than “ma amie” for a female friend?
cards.answer: Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, mon replaces ma for easier pronunciation.

cards.front: What are the six present-tense forms of aller used to build the near future tense?
cards.answer: je vais / tu vas / il/elle/on va / nous allons / vous allez / ils/elles vont

cards.front: What four masculine countries does this lesson list that take “au”?
cards.answer: le Canada / le Sénégal / le Maroc / le Mexique

cards.front: Why is “le Mexique” an exception among French country names ending in -e?
cards.answer: Most countries ending in -e are feminine, but le Mexique is an exception and is masculine, so it takes au.

cards.front: Why does French use “en” for planes, cars and trains but “à” for bikes and walking?
cards.answer: En is used for enclosed transport like planes and cars, while à is used for open or human-powered transport like bikes and walking.

cards.front: What are the six present-tense forms of the irregular verb faire?
cards.answer: je fais / tu fais / il/elle/on fait / nous faisons / vous faites / ils/elles font

cards.front: What six adverbs of frequency does this lesson give for saying how often you do a hobby?
items: de temps en temps (from time to time)
cards.answer: toujours (always) / souvent (often) / quelquefois / parfois (sometimes) / de temps en temps (from time to time) / rarement (rarely) / ne…jamais (never)

cards.front: Why does “faire de la natation” use “de la” while “faire du vélo” uses “du”?
cards.answer: De combines with the article to match the noun's gender, so de + le becomes du while de + la stays de la.

cards.front: Why is it easy to mix up faire de, jouer à and jouer de when talking about hobbies?
cards.answer: Each activity type needs its own preposition: faire de for activities, jouer à for sports and jouer de for instruments.

cards.front: What five qualities does this lesson say a good friend must have (un bon ami doit être...)?
cards.answer: fidèle (loyal) / honnête (honest) / gentil (kind) / patient (patient) / drôle (funny)

cards.front: What three things does this lesson say a good friend must do?
cards.answer: écouter (listen) / encourager (encourage) / soutenir (support)

cards.front: Why does combining the present, past and near future tense strengthen a paragraph about a best friend?
cards.answer: Using the near future alongside the present and past shows a range of tenses across multiple time frames.

cards.front: Why should you use phrases like à mon avis or je trouve que instead of just saying j'aime?
cards.answer: Opinion phrases like à mon avis and je trouve que let you extend your answers beyond simple likes and dislikes.

cards.front: What are the three past-participle endings for -er, -ir and -re verbs in the perfect tense?
cards.answer: -er verbs → -é / -ir verbs → -i / -re verbs → -u

cards.front: What five irregular past participles does this lesson give?
cards.answer: faire → fait (did/made) / voir → vu (saw) / prendre → pris (took) / boire → bu (drank) / écrire → écrit (wrote)

cards.front: Why does “je suis allé(e)” use être while “j'ai visité” uses avoir?
cards.answer: Most verbs use avoir as the auxiliary, but verbs of movement and reflexive verbs use être instead.

cards.front: Why must “elle est allée” add an extra -e compared to “il est allé”?
cards.answer: With être verbs, the past participle must agree with the subject, adding -e for a feminine subject.

cards.front: What four irregular feminine adjective forms does this lesson give?
cards.answer: bon → bonne / beau → belle / nouveau → nouvelle / vieux → vieille

cards.front: What four types of film does this lesson name?
cards.answer: un film d'action (action film) / une comédie (comedy) / un film d'horreur (horror film) / un dessin animé (cartoon)

cards.front: Why does “ennuyeux” become “ennuyeuse” in the feminine when describing a boring film?
cards.answer: Adjectives ending in -eux change to -euse in the feminine form, so ennuyeux becomes ennuyeuse.

cards.front: Why is “MRS VAN DER TRAMP” a useful memory aid in this lesson?
cards.answer: Each letter stands for a French verb of movement that uses être instead of avoir in the perfect tense.

cards.front: What four arguments does this lesson give in favour of marriage?
items: an important tradition in many cultures
gives legal security to the couple
cards.answer: shows a serious commitment / an important tradition in many cultures / gives legal security to the couple / a beautiful celebration of love

cards.front: What four arguments does this lesson give against marriage?
items: marriage costs a lot of money
a PACS is a simpler alternative
cards.answer: not necessary to be happy / marriage costs a lot of money / many marriages end in divorce / a PACS is a simpler alternative

cards.front: Why is le PACS a popular alternative to marriage in France?
cards.answer: The PACS gives many of the same legal rights as marriage but is simpler and cheaper to arrange.

cards.front: Why is “je serais” the correct conditional form of être rather than a regular one?
cards.answer: Être has an irregular conditional stem, ser-, instead of using its infinitive, so “I would be” is je serais.

cards.front: What three ways to say “I would like” does this lesson give for booking a hotel room?
cards.answer: je voudrais / j'aimerais / je souhaite

cards.front: What four types of meal plan does this lesson give for hotels?
cards.answer: petit-déjeuner compris (breakfast included) / en demi-pension (half board) / en pension complète (full board) / tout compris (all-inclusive)

cards.front: Why does using je voudrais or j'aimerais instead of je veux improve a hotel booking request?
cards.answer: Using je voudrais or j'aimerais instead of je veux shows you can use the conditional tense, which makes the request more polite.

cards.front: Why should you use the imperfect tense for describing a hotel room but the perfect tense for what happened?
cards.answer: The imperfect describes what a room was like, while the perfect tense describes events, so mixing both shows strong grammar.

cards.front: What three named jerseys are awarded in the Tour de France, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: maillot jaune – overall leader / maillot vert – best sprinter / maillot à pois – best climber

cards.front: What five imperfect-tense phrases does this lesson give for describing a past sporting event?
cards.answer: c'était + adjective (it was) / il y avait + noun (there was/were) / j'étais + adjective (I was) / il faisait + weather (it was — weather) / je jouais / je faisais (used to)

cards.front: How do you form the imperfect tense from the present tense of a French verb?
cards.answer: Take the nous form of the present tense, remove -ons, and add the imperfect endings.

cards.front: Why is the Tour de France described as a cultural celebration rather than just a sporting event?
cards.answer: Millions of spectators line the roads and towns prepare festivities along the route, making it a cultural celebration too.

cards.front: What four unhealthy habits does this lesson list under “il ne faut pas”?
cards.answer: fumer des cigarettes (smoke cigarettes) / vapoter (vape) / boire de l'alcool (drink alcohol) / manger trop de fast-food (fast food)

cards.front: What six reflexive verbs does this lesson give for talking about health?
cards.answer: se lever (to get up) / se coucher (to go to bed) / se laver (to wash) / se détendre / se relaxer (to relax) / se reposer (to rest) / se sentir (to feel)

cards.front: Why does “il ne faut pas fumer” mean “you must not smoke” rather than “you must smoke”?
cards.answer: Il ne faut pas is the negative form of il faut, so it means “you must not” instead of “you must”.

cards.front: Why might you use il est important de or il est nécessaire de instead of always saying il faut?
cards.answer: Alternatives such as il est important de and il est nécessaire de add variety instead of always repeating il faut.

cards.front: What are the six simple future forms of aller given in this lesson?
cards.answer: j'irai / tu iras / il/elle ira / nous irons / vous irez / ils/elles iront

cards.front: What six forms of transport use “en” in French, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: en avion (by plane) / en voiture (by car) / en train (by train) / en bateau (by boat) / en bus / en autocar (by bus/coach) / en métro (by underground)

cards.front: Why must you write “j'aime la France” with the article “la”, unlike the English “I like France”?
cards.answer: When a verb of opinion is followed by a country name, you must include the definite article, unlike in English.

cards.front: Why does the near future form of weather use “il va” before an infinitive?
cards.answer: Weather in the near future follows the same il va plus infinitive pattern as other near future sentences, such as il va pleuvoir.

cards.front: What four other French celebrations, with their dates, are named besides Christmas, Easter and Bastille Day?
items: la fête de la Musique – 21 June
cards.answer: la fête des Rois – 6 January / la Chandeleur – 2 February / la fête de la Musique – 21 June / la Toussaint – 1 November

cards.front: What six Christmas vocabulary items does this lesson give for Noël in France?
cards.answer: le sapin (Christmas tree) / les cadeaux (presents) / le repas de Noël (Christmas dinner) / la dinde (turkey) / les décorations (decorations) / les chocolats (chocolates)

cards.front: Why is the French Easter tradition of chocolate eggs different from the British Easter Bunny tradition?
cards.answer: In French tradition, church bells fly to Rome on Good Friday and return on Easter Sunday, dropping chocolate eggs in gardens.

cards.front: Why does this lesson highlight France's Muslim population when discussing celebrations?
cards.answer: France has the largest Muslim population in Western Europe, so describing both secular and religious celebrations shows cultural awareness.

cards.front: What four advantages of technology does this lesson give?
items: stay in touch with family and friends
a good way to have fun
cards.answer: communicate easily with people worldwide / useful for homework research / stay in touch with family and friends / a good way to have fun

cards.front: What four disadvantages of technology does this lesson give?
items: too much time in front of the screen
bad for health, not enough exercise
cards.answer: too much time in front of the screen / cyberbullying is a serious problem / bad for health, not enough exercise / a risk of addiction

cards.front: Why might “mon portable” mean either a mobile phone or a laptop in French?
cards.answer: Portable can mean either a mobile phone or a laptop depending on context, though mon portable usually means my phone in everyday conversation.

cards.front: What four time expressions does this lesson give for describing a French wedding?
cards.answer: avant la cérémonie (before the ceremony) / pendant le repas (during the meal) / après les discours (after the speeches) / jusqu'à minuit (until midnight)

cards.front: What four tenses does this lesson use to describe celebrations, with an example verb form for each?
cards.answer: present – je célèbre / perfect – j'ai célébré / near future – je vais célébrer / conditional – je voudrais assister

cards.front: Why does the number of kisses in la bise vary between people in France?
cards.answer: The number of kisses varies by region, from one to five, with some people starting on the left cheek and others the right.

cards.front: Why does “les” come directly before “entendre” in “je ne veux pas les entendre”?
cards.answer: Direct object pronouns normally go before the conjugated verb, but when there is an infinitive, the pronoun goes before the infinitive instead.

cards.front: What are the four French partitive articles used to say “some”, and when is each used?
cards.answer: du – before masculine nouns / de la – before feminine nouns / de l' – before a vowel / des – before plural nouns

cards.front: What are the three main meals named in this lesson?
cards.answer: le petit déjeuner (breakfast) / le déjeuner (lunch) / le dîner (dinner/evening meal)

cards.front: Why does “je mange du poisson” become “je ne mange pas de poisson” in the negative?
cards.answer: After a negative, the partitive article changes to de, or d' before a vowel, so du poisson becomes pas de poisson.

cards.front: Why must French always include du, de la or des before a food word, unlike English?
cards.answer: English often leaves out “some” before food words, but French always requires the partitive article, such as du pain for bread.

cards.front: How does “à” combine with the definite article in “avoir mal à” for each type of noun?
cards.answer: à + le → au (masculine) / à + la → à la (feminine) / à + l' → à l' (vowel) / à + les → aux (plural)

cards.front: What six reflexive verbs for health does this lesson give?
cards.answer: se sentir (to feel) / se reposer (to rest) / se coucher (to go to bed) / se réveiller (to wake up) / se blesser (to injure oneself) / se détendre (to relax)

cards.front: Why does “elle s'est reposée” need an extra -e at the end?
cards.answer: In the passé composé, reflexive verbs always use être, and the past participle agrees with the subject, adding -e for a feminine subject.

cards.front: Why is it “j'ai mal au ventre” but “j'ai mal à la tête”?
cards.answer: Au is the contraction used before a masculine noun like ventre, while à la is used before a feminine noun like tête.

cards.front: What are the four French demonstrative adjectives meaning “this/that/these/those”?
cards.answer: ce – masculine before a consonant / cet – before a vowel/silent h / cette – feminine singular / ces – plural

cards.front: What are the six irregular imperative forms of être and avoir given in this lesson?
cards.answer: sois (être, tu) / soyons (être, nous) / soyez (être, vous) / aie (avoir, tu) / ayons (avoir, nous) / ayez (avoir, vous)

cards.front: Why is it “Écoute!” and not “Écoutes!” when telling one person to listen?
cards.answer: For -er verbs, the imperative tu form drops the final -s, so écouter becomes Écoute rather than Écoutes.

cards.front: Why is “cet acteur” correct instead of “ce acteur”?
cards.answer: Cet replaces ce before a masculine noun that starts with a vowel or silent h, such as acteur.

cards.front: What five types of home does this lesson name?
cards.answer: une maison individuelle (detached house) / un appartement (flat) / une maison jumelée (semi-detached house) / une maison mitoyenne (terraced house) / une ferme (farmhouse)

cards.front: What are the three tense forms of “il y a” (there is/are) given in this lesson?
items: il y aura – there will be (future)
cards.answer: il y a – there is/are (present) / il y avait – there was/were (past) / il y aura – there will be (future)

cards.front: Why do “grand” and “petit” come before the noun while most French adjectives come after it?
cards.answer: Most adjectives come after the noun in French, but common ones like grand, petit, beau, joli and vieux come before it.

cards.front: Why is it “une grande cuisine” but “un petit jardin”?
cards.answer: Adjectives must agree with the noun they describe, so grande matches the feminine cuisine while petit matches the masculine jardin.

cards.front: What five advantages of social media does this lesson give?
cards.answer: stay in contact with friends / free and easy to use / share photos and videos / useful for revision and homework / discover new things

cards.front: What five disadvantages of social media does this lesson give?
items: dangerous — unsure who's behind the screen
cards.answer: too much time spent online / cyberbullying is a serious problem / dangerous — unsure who's behind the screen / can create an addiction / bad for mental health

cards.front: How can you tell whether to use “qui” or “que” in a sentence like “une appli ___ j'utilise”?
cards.answer: If the word after the gap is a verb, use qui; if it is a subject like a pronoun, use que.

cards.front: Why does “que” become “qu'” in “une appli qu'il utilise”?
cards.answer: Que shortens to qu' before a vowel, as in une appli qu'il utilise.

cards.front: What four contractions does this lesson give for à or de combining with le or les?
cards.answer: à + le → au / de + le → du / à + les → aux / de + les → des

cards.front: What four past-participle agreement endings does this lesson give for “allé” with different subjects?
items: il est allé – no extra letter
cards.answer: il est allé – no extra letter / elle est allée – add -e / ils sont allés – add -s / elles sont allées – add -es

cards.front: Why do you say “jouer au football” but “faire du vélo”?
cards.answer: Jouer à is used for team and ball sports like football, while faire de is used for individual sports and activities like cycling.

cards.front: Why does “aller” take être rather than avoir when describing going to a sports event in the past?
cards.answer: Aller is one of the DR MRS P VANDERTRAMP verbs, so it takes être rather than avoir as its auxiliary.

cards.front: What three comparison structures does this lesson give in French?
cards.answer: plus … que (more … than) / moins … que (less … than) / aussi … que (as … as)

cards.front: What six positive adjectives does this lesson give for describing a town?
cards.answer: animé(e) (lively) / touristique (touristy) / pittoresque (picturesque) / propre (clean) / tranquille (quiet) / intéressant(e) (interesting)

cards.front: Why is “meilleur” used instead of “plus bon” when comparing two restaurants?
cards.answer: The adjective bon has an irregular comparative, meilleur, instead of the regular form plus bon.

cards.front: Why does this lesson describe la banlieue as a good compromise between town and countryside?
cards.answer: La banlieue is a good compromise because it is less noisy than the city but more practical than the countryside.

cards.front: What five things does this lesson say a restaurant role-play might ask you to do?
cards.answer: reserve a table / order food / state a dietary requirement / make a complaint / ask for the bill

cards.front: What three question structures does this lesson recommend preparing for a restaurant conversation?
cards.answer: Est-ce que…? / Qu'est-ce que…? / Avez-vous…?

cards.front: Why does “je mange du fromage” become “je ne mange pas de fromage” when ordering food?
cards.answer: After a negative, the partitive article always changes to de or d', so du fromage becomes pas de fromage.

cards.front: Why should you prepare set question structures before a restaurant role-play conversation?
cards.answer: One task in a restaurant conversation always requires you to ask a question, so structures like Est-ce que should be ready in advance.

cards.front: What four ways does this lesson give to express obligation about the environment, from strongest to weakest?
cards.answer: il faut (one must) / on doit (we must) / on devrait (one should) / tout le monde devrait (everyone should)

cards.front: What are the six future-tense endings that are the same for every French verb?
cards.answer: -ai (je) / -as (tu) / -a (il/elle) / -ons (nous) / -ez (vous) / -ont (ils/elles)

cards.front: Why are the future-tense endings the same for every French verb even though the stems differ?
cards.answer: The future endings are the same for all verbs; only the stem differs, using the infinitive for regular verbs and a special stem for irregular ones.

cards.front: Why is “il fera” the correct future form of faire rather than one based on the infinitive?
cards.answer: Faire has an irregular future stem, fer-, so “it will be” (weather) is il fera rather than a regular infinitive-based form.

cards.front: What five time-telling expressions does this lesson give, besides just naming the hour?
cards.answer: et quart (quarter past) / et demie (half past) / moins le quart (quarter to) / midi (midday) / minuit (midnight)

cards.front: What six positive adjectives does this lesson give for describing a school subject?
cards.answer: intéressant(e) (interesting) / passionnant(e) (exciting) / utile (useful) / pratique (practical) / facile (easy) / amusant(e) (fun)

cards.front: Why does French use the 24-hour clock for a school timetable but the 12-hour clock in everyday conversation?
cards.answer: French uses the 24-hour clock in formal contexts like timetables and transport, but the 12-hour clock in everyday conversation.

cards.front: Why does “la prof est stricte” need an extra -e that “le prof est strict” does not?
cards.answer: Adjectives describing teachers must agree in gender, so the feminine la prof adds an -e that the masculine le prof does not need.

cards.front: What four structures does this lesson give for expressing obligation, permission or prohibition at school?
items: il est interdit de (it is forbidden to)
cards.answer: il faut (you must) / on doit (you must) / il est interdit de (it is forbidden to) / on ne peut pas (you cannot)

cards.front: What six “il est + adjective + de” expressions does this lesson give for school rules?
cards.answer: il est nécessaire de (necessary) / il est essentiel de (essential) / il est important de (important) / il est permis de (allowed) / il est impossible de (impossible) / il est indispensable de (vital)

cards.front: Why does “il y a une piscine” become “il n'y a pas de piscine” in the negative?
cards.answer: After il n'y a pas, the article always changes to de or d', regardless of the noun's gender.

cards.front: Why does this lesson say wearing a school uniform can lead to less bullying?
cards.answer: Wearing the same uniform as everyone else means students are dressed the same way, which this lesson says leads to less bullying.

title: Jobs, Work Experience and Future Plans

cards.front: What three common patterns does this lesson give for changing a masculine job title to feminine?
cards.answer: -eur → -euse (e.g. coiffeur/coiffeuse) / -ier → -ière (e.g. infirmier/infirmière) / -teur → -trice (e.g. acteur/actrice)

cards.front: What six irregular conditional stems does this lesson give?
cards.answer: être → ser- / avoir → aur- / faire → fer- / aller → ir- / vouloir → voudr- / pouvoir → pourr-

cards.front: Why is “un(e) médecin” written the same for both a male and a female doctor, unlike “coiffeur/coiffeuse”?
cards.answer: Some traditionally masculine job nouns like médecin are now used for both genders, unlike words that change pattern such as coiffeur/coiffeuse.

cards.front: Why is “je ferais” the correct conditional form of faire rather than a regular infinitive-based form?
cards.answer: Faire has an irregular conditional stem, fer-, so “I would do” is je ferais instead of a regular infinitive-based form.
